title: Review: telling about a weekend
why: The review of the unit on the past: you bring together the perfecto and the indefinido, regular and irregular, and learn to choose between them using the time marker. With primero, luego, después and al final, you can tell about a whole weekend smoothly, like on Monday morning at the office.

{"lessons": ["

Perfecto or indefinido: the time marker decides

You now have two tenses for the past: “I've done” and “I did”. English has the same pair and the logic is close, with one big difference: Spain uses the perfecto for anything that happened today, even “this morning” once the morning is over. The principle: is the period in which the action happened over or not?

Perfecto: period not overIndefinido: period over
hoy (today)ayer, anteayer, anoche
esta mañana, esta tardeel lunes, el sábado pasado
esta semana, este mesla semana pasada, el mes pasado
este año, este veranoel año pasado, en 2019, en agosto
ya, todavía nohace dos días, hace un año
nunca, alguna vez, muchas vecesun día, el verano de 2018
Esta mañana he desayunado en casa, pero ayer desayuné en una cafetería.This morning I had breakfast at home, but yesterday I had it in a café.

The weekend case

On Monday, the weekend is over: people ask ¿Qué tal el fin de semana? ¿Qué hiciste? and answer in the indefinido: El sábado fui al cine. On Sunday evening, on the other hand, it isn't over yet: Este fin de semana he descansado mucho.

If you're unsure, look for the time marker in the sentence. No marker at all? If the action has just happened or still affects the present (¿Qué ha dicho?, He perdido las llaves), use the perfecto, just like “What has he said?” or “I've lost my keys” in English. If you're telling a story that's over and done with, use the indefinido.

", "

Telling things in order

To tell about your weekend, you need a few little words that organize the story. They work like their English equivalents and usually go at the beginning of the sentence.

SpanishEnglishExample
primerofirstPrimero desayunamos en el hotel.
luegothen, nextLuego fuimos al Retiro.
despuésafter that, afterwardsDespués comimos en un bar.
más tardelaterMás tarde vimos una película.
al finalin the end, finallyAl final volvimos a casa a las doce.

Después de + infinitive = “after …ing”: Después de comer, dimos un paseo (after eating, we went for a walk). English uses the -ing form, Spanish a plain infinitive.

A weekend, told

El sábado me levanté tarde. Primero hice la compra, luego comí con mis padres y después fui al cine con Elena. Al final volví a casa muy cansado. Hoy he dormido hasta las diez.On Saturday I got up late. First I did the grocery shopping, then I had lunch with my parents, and after that I went to the movies with Elena. In the end I came home very tired. Today I slept until ten.

The whole Saturday story is in the indefinido; only the last sentence, with hoy, switches to the perfecto (even though English says “slept” here).

Watch the meaning of comer: in Spain, it means “to eat”, but also “to have lunch” (the midday meal, around 2 p.m.): comí con mis padres = I had lunch with my parents. La comida is lunch. Dinner is la cena.

", "

Forms not to mix up

Here, side by side, are the two past tenses of key verbs for telling a story. Recite them out loud: it's the best way to lock them in.

ir: perfectoir: indefinidohacer: perfectohacer: indefinido
yohe idofuihe hechohice
túhas idofuistehas hechohiciste
él, ella, ustedha idofueha hechohizo
nosotros, nosotrashemos idofuimoshemos hechohicimos
vosotros, vosotrashabéis idofuisteishabéis hechohicisteis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshan idofueronhan hechohicieron

The most common mistakes

WrongRightWhy
fuí, diófui, dioone syllable: no accent
hicistes, fuisteshiciste, fuisteno final -s with tú
dijierondijeronafter j, the ending is -eron
llegé, empezéllegué, empecéspelling before -é
ayer he comidoayer comíayer is a finished period
hoy comíhoy he comidohoy isn't over (Madrid usage)

For the verb estar, remember the pair he estado / estuve: ¿Has estado alguna vez en Segovia? — Sí, estuve allí el año pasado. The question is about experience (perfecto), the answer gives a date (indefinido), exactly like “Have you ever been…? — Yes, I was there last year.”
